(6)
parts.mark_scheme:

A1: Correct expression for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\sqrt3\mathrm{e}^{x\sqrt3}\sin3x+3\mathrm{e}^{x\sqrt3}\cos3x$
M1: Sets their $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, factorises out or divides by $\mathrm{e}^{x\sqrt3}$ producing an equation in $\sin3x$ and $\cos3x$
A1: Achieves either $\tan3x=-\sqrt3$ or $\tan3x=-\dfrac{3}{\sqrt3}$
M1: Correct order of arctan, followed by $\div3$ (accept $3x=\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{5\pi}{9}$ or $3x=\dfrac{-\pi}{3}\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-\pi}{9}$ but not $x=\arctan(\frac{-\sqrt3}{3})$)
A1: cso $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{9}$; ignore extra solutions outside the range, withhold mark for extra inside the range

Alternative using the form $R\sin(3x+\alpha)$, just last 3 marks: A1: Achieves either $(\sqrt{12})\sin(3x+\frac{\pi}{3})=0$ or $(\sqrt{12})\cos(3x-\frac{\pi}{6})=0$; M1: correct order of arcsin/arccos to produce a value of $x$; A1: cao $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{9}$

Alternative to part (a) squaring both sides, just last 3 marks: A1: $\sqrt3\sin3x=-3\cos3x\Rightarrow \cos^2(3x)=\frac14$ or $\sin^2(3x)=\frac34$; M1: $x=\frac13\arccos(\pm\sqrt{\frac14})$ oe; A1: $x=\dfrac{2\pi}{9}$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Alternative using $R\sin(3x+\alpha)$: M1 Correct order of arcsin or arcos, etc to produce a value of x. Eg accept $3x+\frac{\pi}{3}=0$ or $\pi$ or $2\pi\Rightarrow x=....$ A1 Cao $x=\frac{2\pi}{9}$ Ignore extra solutions outside the range. Withhold mark for extra inside the range.

questions.stem:
The functions f and g are defined by
$\mathrm{f}:x\mapsto \mathrm{e}^x+2, \quad x\in\mathbb{R}$
$\mathrm{g}:x\mapsto \ln x, \quad x>0$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) State the range of f.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: Range of $\mathrm{f}(x)>2$. Accept $y>2$, $(2,\infty)$, $\mathrm{f}>2$, as well as 'range is the set of numbers bigger than 2' but don't accept $x>2$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find $\mathrm{fg}(x)$, giving your answer in its simplest form.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: For applying the correct order of operations; look for $\mathrm{e}^{\ln x}+2$ (note $\ln \mathrm{e}^x+2$ is M0)
A1: Simplifies $\mathrm{e}^{\ln x}+2$ to $x+2$; just the answer is acceptable for both marks

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find the exact value of $x$ for which $\mathrm{f}(2x+3)=6$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Starts with $\mathrm{e}^{2x+3}+2=6$ and proceeds to $\mathrm{e}^{2x+3}=\ldots$
A1: $\mathrm{e}^{2x+3}=4$
M1: Takes ln's both sides, $2x+3=\ln\ldots$, and proceeds to $x=\ldots$
A1: $x=\dfrac{\ln4-3}{2}$ oe e.g. $\ln2-\dfrac32$; remember to isw any incorrect working after a correct answer

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Find $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$, the inverse function of f, stating its domain.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Starts with $y=\mathrm{e}^x+2$ or $x=\mathrm{e}^y+2$ and attempts to change the subject (all ln work must be correct; the 2 must be dealt with first; e.g. $y=\mathrm{e}^x+2\Rightarrow\ln y=x+\ln2\Rightarrow x=\ln y-\ln2$ is M0)
A1: $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)=\ln(x-2)$ or $y=\ln(x-2)$ or $y=\ln|x-2|$; there must be some form of bracket
B1ft: Either $x>2$, or follow through on their answer to part (a), provided that it wasn't $y\in\mathbb{R}$. Do not accept $y>2$ or $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)>2$

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) On the same axes sketch the curves with equation $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$ and $y=\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$, giving the coordinates of all the points where the curves cross the axes.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: Shape for $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$. The graph should only lie in quadrants 1 and 2. It should start out with a gradient that is approx. 0 above the $x$ axis in quadrant 2 and increase in gradient as it moves into quadrant 1. You should not see a minimum point on the graph.
B1: $(0,3)$ lies on the curve; accept 3 written on the $y$-axis as long as the point lies on the curve
B1: Shape for $y=\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$. The graph should only lie in quadrants 4 and 1. It should start out with gradient that is approx. infinite to the right of the $y$-axis in quadrant 4 and decrease in gradient as it moves into quadrant 1. You should not see a maximum point. Also withhold this mark if it intersects $y=\mathrm{e}^x$
B1: $(3,0)$ lies on the curve; accept 3 written on the $x$-axis as long as the point lies on the curve
Condone lack of labels in this part.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Examples: Scores 1,0,1,0. Both shapes are fine, do not be concerned about asymptotes appearing at x=2, y=2. (See notes) Both co-ordinates are incorrect
- Scores 0,1,1,1 Shape for $y=e^x$ is incorrect, there is a minimum point on the graph. All other marks an be awarded

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Differentiate with respect to $x$,
(i) $x^{\frac12}\ln(3x)$

(ii) $\dfrac{1-10x}{(2x-1)^5}$, giving your answer in its simplest form.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(i) M1: Attempts to differentiate $\ln(3x)$ to $\dfrac{B}{x}$ (note $\dfrac{1}{3x}$ is fine): $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\ln(3x))=\dfrac{3}{3x}$
M1: Attempts the product rule for $x^{\frac12}\ln(3x)$ (if the rule is quoted it must be correct, with some attempt to differentiate both terms; if not quoted nor implied only accept answers of the form $\ln(3x)\times Ax^{-\frac12}+x^{\frac12}\times\dfrac{B}{x}$, $A,B>0$)
A1: Any correct (unsimplified) form of the answer: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{\frac12}\ln(3x))=\ln(3x)\times\dfrac12x^{-\frac12}+x^{\frac12}\times\dfrac{3}{3x}=\left(\dfrac{\ln(3x)}{2\sqrt x}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt x}\right)=x^{-\frac12}\left(\dfrac12\ln3x+1\right)$. Note this part does not require the answer to be in its simplest form; remember to isw any incorrect further work.

(ii) M1: Applies the quotient rule (a version of which appears in the formula booklet); if quoted must be correct with an attempt to differentiate both terms; if not quoted nor implied only accept answers of the form $\dfrac{(2x-1)^5\times\pm10-(1-10x)\times C(2x-1)^4}{(2x-1)^{10\text{ or }7\text{ or }25}}$
A1: Any unsimplified form of the answer, e.g. $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{(2x-1)^5\times-10-(1-10x)\times5(2x-1)^4\times2}{((2x-1)^5)^2}$
A1: cao. Must be simplified as required: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{80x}{(2x-1)^6}$

Alt using the product rule: writes $\dfrac{1-10x}{(2x-1)^5}$ as $(1-10x)(2x-1)^{-5}$ and applies $vu'+uv'$: M1A1 for $(2x-1)^{-5}\times-10+(1-10x)\times-5(2x-1)^{-6}\times2$, A1 simplifies as main scheme to $80x(2x-1)^{-6}$ or equivalent.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Given that $x=3\tan2y$ find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ in terms of $x$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:

A1: Writes down $\dfrac{dx}{dy}=6\sec^22y$ or implicitly to get $1=6\sec^22y\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ (accept from the quotient rule $\dfrac{6}{\cos^22y}$ or even $\dfrac{\cos2y\times6\cos2y-3\sin2y\times-2\sin2y}{\cos^22y}$)
M1: An attempt to invert 'their' $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ to reach $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\mathrm{f}(y)$, or changes the subject of their implicit differential to achieve a similar result $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\mathrm{f}(y)$
M1: Replaces an expression for $\sec^22y$ in their $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ or $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ with $x$ by attempting to use $\sec^22y=1+\tan^22y$. Alternatively, replaces an expression for $y$ in $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$ or $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ with $\frac12\arctan(\frac{x}{3})$
A1: Any correct form of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ in terms of $x$: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{6\left(1+\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)^2\right)}=\left(\dfrac{3}{18+2x^2}\right)$

Alt using arctan: rearrange $x=3\tan2y$ to $y=\frac12\arctan(\frac{x}{3})$ and attempt to differentiate: M1A1 for rearranging and attempting, then M1,A2 for differentiating to a form $\dfrac{A}{1+(\frac{x}{3})^2}=\frac12\times\dfrac{1}{(1+(\frac{x}{3})^2)}\times\frac13$ or $\dfrac{1}{6(1+(\frac{x}{3})^2)}$ oe.
